areas.name: How city government performs
areas.dek: Every September the mayor's office publishes the Mayor's Management Report, the measures agencies report about their own work. These tools follow those numbers over decades, track what laws and audits require agencies to do and grade the city on its answers to 311.

picks.name: NYC Pulse
picks.summary: Twenty-nine years of Mayor's Management Report measures, fiscal 1998 to 2026, in searchable charts by agency, measure and neighborhood, with dollar figures adjusted for inflation. Every value links to the page it came from.
picks.why: It shows long-run trends the official report does not, and it shows its work. The fiscal 2026 numbers went in within days of their release.
questions: Are 911 response times getting better or worse?
How has this agency changed since the 2000s?
picks.caveat: New this year and built by one journalist with AI coding help; the site warns that linking old reports to new data can introduce errors. The report measures what agencies choose to measure.
picks.data: Mayor's Management Report indicators, from NYC Open Data and printed reports since 1998
index: Is the city getting better at its basic jobs?

picks.name: NYC Council Legislation Trackers
picks.summary: Every local law passed since 2014, read for each duty it places on a city agency, what it was estimated to cost and what new powers it granted: 8,261 obligations from 2,138 laws, with the agency, deadline and exact legal language.
picks.why: It turns the city's laws into a to-do list, so anyone can check what an agency was told to do and whether a required report is late. Quotes are checked against the law text.
questions: What reports is this agency required to publish?
What did this local law actually require?
picks.caveat: Extraction is AI-assisted, and about a quarter of obligations are not tied to a specific agency. Alerts and a question feature are for paying members.
picks.data: Enacted local laws and Council fiscal impact statements
index: What does a law require an agency to do?

picks.name: The audit files
picks.summary: Collects every watchdog report on New York City government since January 2025 (city and state comptroller audits, Department of Investigation reports, court monitors and oversight boards) and restates what each examined, found and recommended, with implementation status. Filter by watchdog, topic or unfixed recommendations and open any card for the official report.
picks.why: It follows every watchdog report on city government since January 2025, from both comptrollers, the Department of Investigation and court-appointed monitors, to whether its recommendations were carried out.
questions: What have auditors found wrong at a city agency this year?
Did the agency actually fix what the comptroller told it to fix?
picks.caveat: Summaries are machine-written from the official reports; check the linked report before quoting a finding.
picks.data: NYC and NYS comptroller audits, DOI reports, court-monitor and oversight-board reports, January 2025 onward
index: Did the city fix what its auditors found?

picks.name: Overdue
picks.summary: Every report a city agency is legally required to file, about 2,200 of them, marked never filed, overdue, up to date, completed or waived, from the records department's own lists, refreshed weekly.
picks.why: It turns the city's official list of required reports into a scorecard of which agencies file what they owe, with each report linked to its filings page.
questions: Which agencies are late on the reports the law requires?
Has a report I care about ever been filed?
picks.caveat: Statuses are computed from stated frequencies and recorded filing dates, so they are estimates; the official record is the records department's portal. Overlaps the Council legislation trackers, which read the laws themselves.
picks.data: Required Reports and Government Publications lists, Department of Records (NYC Open Data)
index: Which agencies are late on required reports?

bench.name: MuckRock: New York City
bench.summary: Response times, success rates and full correspondence for public records requests filed with city agencies through MuckRock: a 196-day average response across 2,679 requests.
bench.why: The only independent view of how well each agency answers Freedom of Information Law requests.
bench.caveat: Covers only requests filed through MuckRock.

bench.name: Who's who in the Mamdani administration
bench.summary: A running, dated roster of Mayor Mamdani's senior hires, from the deputy mayors to the commissioners and agency heads, with a short background on each and the date City Hall announced the appointment.
bench.why: The only current, maintained roster of who runs the city's agencies; the independent appointee trackers have stalled.
bench.caveat: Compiled from City Hall announcements, so it has no method note, no download and no record of departures. About 40 top positions, not the full leadership of every agency.

bench.name: Mamdani transcript search
bench.summary: A searchable archive of the mayor's on-the-record statements since Jan. 1, 2026: speeches, press conferences, press releases and executive orders, about 1,400 items, refreshed daily.
bench.why: The only place to search everything the mayor has said officially, in one box.
bench.caveat: Built from nyc.gov and public broadcasts; items are labeled by source.

official.name: Measuring NYC Government Performance
official.summary: Color-coded cards for 17 agencies showing whether key measures improved or worsened over the past month, three months, year to date and against 2019.
official.why: The quickest read on which way agencies are heading, from an independently elected office, and more current than the management report.
questions: Is the city fixing things faster than last year?
Is this agency doing better than before Covid?
official.caveat: Covers a chosen subset of measures, and a few cards show missing or stale values.
official.data: Mayor's Management Report indicators and other agency open data
official.freshness: Updated as data posts; most measures refreshed Sept. 24-27, 2026
index: Which agencies are improving and which are slipping?

official.name: Audit Recommendations Tracker
official.summary: Every recommendation from comptroller audits since January 2022, whether the agency agreed and whether it says it followed through.
official.why: It follows audits past the headline to whether anything changed, which almost no one else tracks.
official.caveat: Status is as reported by the agencies.

official.name: Dynamic Mayor's Management Report
official.summary: The official management report in interactive form, with measures by agency and service, maps and comparisons.
official.why: The source every performance tool builds on, with official definitions for each measure.

official.maker: Department of Records and Information Services
official.name: NYC OpenRecords
official.summary: The city's portal for records requests, with a public search of more than 645,000 past requests and many released records.
official.why: Check whether someone already asked for the records you want, and read what the city handed over.

areas.name: Crime and policing
areas.dek: The Police Department posts crime numbers every week through CompStat. The tools here put those numbers in context for any precinct or Council district, cover every category of complaint rather than just major felonies, track shootings since 2006 and gather what is on the record for individual officers.

picks.name: CompStat Decoder
picks.summary: The Police Department's weekly CompStat numbers for the past 52 weeks against the year before, for the city, every precinct and every Council district, with the patterns and outliers spelled out in plain sentences.
picks.why: It turns the weekly CompStat report into context anyone can read for their own precinct or district, flags which changes stand out and can send updates by email.
questions: How is crime changing near me over the past year?
Which precincts saw the sharpest increases?
picks.caveat: It covers the seven major felonies CompStat tracks, and weekly counts are preliminary.
picks.data: Police Department weekly CompStat reports
index: How is crime changing near me?

picks.name: NYC Quarterly Complaints Dashboard
picks.summary: Every category of crime complaint the Police Department records, from murder to petit larceny and harassment, by quarter, for the city, any borough or precinct, the subway or public housing.
picks.why: It goes well beyond the seven major felonies CompStat leads with, down to the precinct, the subway and public housing, with open code and data.
questions: Is crime up or down in my precinct this year?
What is happening with misdemeanors and lesser offenses?
picks.caveat: Quarterly, so it runs up to three months behind; the CompStat Decoder is fresher for recent weeks.
picks.data: Police Department complaint data (NYC Open Data)
picks.freshness: Quarterly; data through June 2026, updated Aug. 14, 2026
index: Is crime up in my precinct?

picks.name: NYC Shootings
picks.summary: Every shooting the Police Department has recorded since 2006, as a rolling one-year count and a year-to-date race against past years, by borough, precinct, neighborhood and public housing development, with a map.
picks.why: The most complete current view of shootings in the city, down to the precinct and the housing development, with a detailed methods note and a published correction.
questions: Are shootings at a record low?
How many shootings have there been in my precinct this year?
picks.caveat: Runs a quarter behind because the Police Department publishes shooting data quarterly. Neighborhood and housing counts depend on the maker's mapping rules.
picks.data: Police Department shooting incidents, victims and offenders (NYC Open Data)
index: Are shootings going down?

picks.name: Law Enforcement Look Up
picks.summary: A searchable archive of misconduct records on police officers and city correction officers: complaint allegations, internal discipline, lawsuits, findings by judges and prosecutors that an officer was not credible, and news coverage.
picks.why: It is the only public tool that also covers correction officers at Rikers and credibility findings by judges and prosecutors, and it publishes its raw data every week.
questions: Has a judge ever found this officer not credible?
Has this correction officer been disciplined?
picks.caveat: Built by a public defender's office for its own lawyers, so it is harder to use than 50-a.org. Records are not merged by officer; you confirm a match yourself.
picks.data: Complaint review board, police and correction discipline, lawsuits, court and prosecutor credibility records
index: Has a correction officer at Rikers been disciplined?

bench.name: Crime Index
bench.summary: Monthly counts of murders, robberies, assaults, burglaries and thefts in New York City since 2018, charted next to a national sample of about 565 police agencies, with the change so far this year.
bench.why: The best yardstick for whether a New York City trend is local or national, updated monthly.
questions: Is crime in New York City going up or down this year?
Is the drop in murders here bigger than the national drop?
bench.caveat: Citywide only, with FBI crime definitions, so counts will not match CompStat.
bench.data: Police Department monthly crime counts, compiled with other agencies' and the FBI's
index: Is crime going up or down?

bench.maker: Maker not named on the site
bench.name: 50-a.org
bench.summary: Search any current or former police officer by name or badge number and get one page with the officer's civilian complaints, department discipline, lawsuits, rank history and pay.
bench.why: The simplest way to see an officer's full record on one page, current to this month, with every source listed.
questions: Has the officer who stopped me drawn complaints before?
Has this officer been sued or disciplined?
bench.caveat: Included by the editor's judgment: the site does not say who runs it, which is the one test it fails. Complaints still under investigation are missing, and lawsuits list officers who were named even if the claims were later dropped.
bench.data: Civilian Complaint Review Board records, Police Department discipline and trial decisions, Law Department lawsuits, city payroll
index: What is on the record for a particular officer?

bench.name: Atlas of American Gun Violence
bench.summary: A national map of more than 450,000 shootings, searchable by address or neighborhood, with trends by month or year.
bench.why: The easiest way to see shootings near a particular block over time, from a nonprofit newsroom that covers gun violence full time.
bench.caveat: Counts come from the Gun Violence Archive, not the Police Department, so they will not match city figures.

bench.name: Stop-and-Frisk Data
bench.summary: Police stops year by year since 2002: how many, how many ended with no arrest or summons, and the race of the people stopped.
bench.why: The clearest long view of stop-and-frisk for a general reader.
bench.caveat: The chart and download now include 2025, though the text still calls 2024 the latest year. The civil liberties union sued over stop-and-frisk; the figures are the Police Department's.

bench.name: NYPD Vehicle Stops Tracker
bench.summary: Monthly police vehicle stops by command, with the share that end in a summons, arrest or search, driver demographics and a map of recent stops.
bench.why: The clearest public view of traffic stops by precinct, from the Police Department's own stop reports.
bench.caveat: Data run a quarter behind and rely on reports officers file.

bench.name: Crime Data Explorer
bench.summary: Every major crime category since 1993 for the city, any borough, precinct or neighborhood, with year-against-year comparisons and complaints or arrests.
bench.why: The longest view of crime by precinct anywhere, back to 1993, with 2025 the latest complete year.
bench.caveat: Included by the editor's judgment: the tool does not say which datasets its counts come from, the one test it fails.

official.name: Data Transparency Initiative
official.summary: Dashboards from the independent agency that investigates police misconduct, counting complaints and allegations by year, precinct, type and outcome.
official.why: The authoritative current source on whether complaints against police are rising in a precinct, straight from the investigators.

official.name: CompStat 2.0
official.summary: The Police Department's weekly crime statistics for the city, each borough and each precinct, with this year against last and a map of incidents.
official.why: The fastest and most detailed public crime numbers, down to the precinct. No independent tool has replaced it.

official.name: 911 response times
official.summary: Weekly dashboards that break every 911 response into stages, from answering the call to arrival, for police, fire and medical emergencies.
official.why: The only current public measure of how long help takes to arrive. We found no independent alternative.

official.name: Subway crime
official.summary: Major felonies in the transit system by month and type, as raw counts or per million riders.
official.why: The per-rider rate answers the question riders have, which raw counts in news stories do not.

official.name: Hate Crimes Dashboard
official.summary: Hate crime incidents by precinct, bias type and charge, with quarterly summaries of complaints and arrests.
official.why: The only precinct-level hate crime source for the city.

areas.name: Jails and courts
areas.dek: About 6,600 people were in city jails on Sept. 27, 2026, and the city faces a legal deadline of Aug. 31, 2027, to close the jails on Rikers Island. These tools track the jail population, conditions inside and what happens to cases before trial. We found no working public data dashboard from any of the five district attorneys.

picks.maker: Data Collaborative for Justice, John Jay College
picks.name: New York City Jail Population Tracker
picks.summary: The daily jail population since 2016, broken down by case status, race, gender and mental health designation, with a one-year projection and a plain explainer on the plan to close Rikers.
picks.why: It is current to the day, publishes its method and data, and keeps the daily history that the Department of Correction's own open data overwrites.
questions: How many people are in city jails right now?
Is the population low enough to close Rikers?
How many of them have not been convicted?
picks.caveat: The app is slow to load and its tab menu is easy to miss. Its makers support closing Rikers, and the projection assumes no change in policy.
picks.data: Department of Correction daily custody, admission and discharge data; Police Department arrests
index: How many people are in jail right now?
Is the city on track to close Rikers?

picks.maker: New York City Criminal Justice Agency
picks.name: Pretrial Data Dashboards
picks.summary: Six dashboards on what happens between arrest and verdict: how many people are prosecuted, how many await trial at home, how many are rearrested while released and how cases end.
picks.why: Each opens with a plain question and numbers through July 2026, which puts the argument over bail on data instead of anecdote.
questions: Do people released before trial get arrested again?
How do criminal cases usually end?
picks.caveat: Included by the editor's judgment: it names its sources only as court data, not the datasets. The agency is city-funded and advises judges on release, so it is part of the system it measures.
picks.data: The agency's own records on prosecuted arrests and case outcomes
index: Do people released before trial get rearrested?

picks.name: New York Criminal Justice System Data Hub
picks.summary: A daily snapshot of the jail population by race, charge, custody status and length of stay, plus statewide tabs on pretrial release and parole.
picks.why: The best way to see how long people have been held and on what charges, with downloads and a statewide view.
picks.caveat: Only the jail tab is current; the pretrial and parole tabs run one to two years behind. Vera supports closing Rikers.
questions: How long have people in city jails been held?
What charges are people in jail facing?
picks.data: Department of Correction daily custody data (NYC Open Data), archived daily by Vera
index: How long do people stay in jail?

picks.name: CANY Data Portal
picks.summary: Eight dashboards on state prisons: population, releases, deaths, staffing and self-harm, with releases filterable to people sent from New York City.
picks.why: The best public window on state prisons and parole releases, where many city cases end up, with methods and limits spelled out.
picks.caveat: Covers state prisons, not city jails.
questions: How many New Yorkers are in state prison?
How are people being released from prison?
picks.data: State prison agency data (DOCCS)
picks.freshness: About every three months; releases through May 2026
index: How many New Yorkers are in state prison?

bench.name: Tracking Deaths in NYC Jails Since 2022
bench.summary: A running list of every person who has died in city jail custody since 2022, with name, age, date, facility and what happened.
bench.why: The only source that names each person, which the counts elsewhere do not.
bench.caveat: Included by the editor's judgment: when checked on Sept. 28, 2026, it was one death behind the news. It relies on news reports and official statements, and Vera supports closing Rikers.

official.name: Department of Correction Dashboard
official.summary: One page on conditions in city jails: violence, use of force, officers out sick, deaths in custody, missed medical appointments, court appearances and length of stay, each marked as improving or worsening.
official.why: It is the only place that sets violence, staffing, health care and deaths side by side, with a source note under every chart, from an office independent of the mayor.
questions: How violent is Rikers right now?
How many people have died in city jails this year?
Are correction officers showing up to work?
official.caveat: Included by the editor's judgment: the page was last updated July 10, 2026, and its figures lag the department's own open data by months.
official.data: Department of Correction and Correctional Health Services reports, city payroll
index: How violent are the jails?

official.name: Board of Correction dashboards
official.summary: One-page reports on the daily jail census by facility and time in custody, overcrowded housing units and self-injury rates.
official.why: Fresh numbers from the independent jail oversight board on things other tools skip, such as how many housing units exceed its crowding limits.
official.caveat: Static PDFs full of unexplained facility codes.

official.name: Data Insights
official.summary: The department's own daily dashboard of population, admissions, time in custody, charges and violence, compared with the same period last year.
official.why: The freshest official numbers on jail violence.

official.maker: New York State Unified Court System
official.name: Caseload Trends Dashboard
official.summary: Cases filed, resolved and pending, and trials started, in every state trial court since 2019, by court and county.
official.why: The only regular public measure of court backlogs, which drive long jail stays.

official.maker: New York State Unified Court System
official.name: Pretrial Release Data
official.summary: Every arraignment release decision in the state since 2020: release, bail or remand, and whether the person was rearrested.
official.why: The official data researchers use to judge the 2019 bail law.

official.name: Monthly Flash Indicators
official.summary: A monthly report on child welfare and youth justice, including admissions to juvenile detention and the detention population.
official.why: The only current, regular source on youth detention in the city.

areas.name: Housing, homelessness and buildings
areas.dek: The city records every housing violation and the courts record every eviction case, but one building at a time. The tools here connect those records: a landlord's whole portfolio, eviction trends by ZIP code, where affordable housing is getting built and how many people sleep in shelters each night.

picks.name: Who Owns What
picks.summary: Type an address to find the landlord behind a building and every other building tied to the same owner, with violations, complaints, eviction filings, sales and estimated rent-stabilized apartments across the portfolio.
picks.why: It answers the question tenants ask most, with one search and no login, and nothing the city offers shows a landlord's full footprint. The method is documented and the code is open.
questions: Who owns my building?
What else does my landlord own, and is it in bad shape?
Has my building lost rent-stabilized apartments?
picks.caveat: Portfolios are inferred by matching the names and addresses owners report, so owners can be lumped together or split apart. Rent-stabilized counts are estimates from tax bills.
picks.data: Housing Preservation and Development registrations and violations, Buildings Department filings, court eviction records, property sales
index: Who owns my building?
Is my landlord a bad landlord?

picks.name: NYC Shelter Tracker
picks.summary: The city's shelter population day by day, plus monthly totals across every shelter system, including domestic violence shelters and the emergency centers opened for migrants.
picks.why: The city reports these counts in scattered PDFs and separate reports. City Limits combines them, explains what each one includes and posts its data and code.
questions: How many people are in city shelters right now?
How many are families with children?
picks.caveat: The combined monthly total lags about two months.
picks.data: Department of Homeless Services daily reports; shelter reports required by local law
index: How many people are in shelters?

picks.name: Eviction Tracking: New York City
picks.summary: Monthly eviction filings in the city against a 2023-24 baseline, a ZIP code map of filings, the typical amount landlords sue for and a breakdown by neighborhood demographics.
picks.why: A neutral academic presentation with a clear baseline, so you can tell whether filings are high or low, and it compares New York with other cities.
questions: Are evictions rising?
Which ZIP codes see the most eviction cases?
picks.caveat: Counts cases filed, not evictions carried out.
picks.data: State court eviction filings, via the Housing Data Coalition; Census data
index: Are evictions going up?

picks.name: New York City Housing Tracker
picks.summary: A card for each Council district that ranks how much affordable housing it produced from 2014 to 2025, alongside vacancy, rent burden, public housing repair needs and code violations.
picks.why: It turns citywide production data into a district ranking a voter can read in a minute. Nothing official does that.
questions: How much affordable housing has my Council district built?
Is my district doing its share?
picks.caveat: The conference advocates for affordable housing, and its members include developers and lenders. Rankings count units built, not need.
picks.data: Housing Preservation and Development production data and other city open data
index: Is my neighborhood building affordable housing?

bench.maker: Association for Neighborhood and Housing Development
bench.name: DAP Portal
bench.summary: Every public record on a building on one page: sales, financing, violations, permits, lawsuits and evictions, with downloads.
bench.why: The deepest free building record anywhere, and the next click after Who Owns What.
bench.caveat: Dense, and court records require a sign-in. The association is a tenant and community development coalition.

bench.name: NYCHA Repair Needs Tracker
bench.summary: Estimated repair needs for each public housing development, from the Housing Authority's 2023 assessment, searchable by development.
bench.why: It makes a huge, hard-to-read Housing Authority document usable one development at a time.
bench.caveat: Long-term repair estimates, not daily conditions such as heat or elevator outages.

bench.maker: Housing Justice for All and JustFix
bench.name: Good Cause NYC
bench.summary: Enter an address and answer a few questions to learn whether an apartment is likely covered by the 2024 Good Cause Eviction law, with a rent increase calculator.
bench.why: It answers a question the new law created that no city tool answers.
bench.caveat: Built by tenant advocates; not legal advice.

bench.name: Elevator Advocate
bench.summary: Any building's elevator complaint history from the Buildings Department, with its owner, managing agent and Council member, and a ranking of the buildings with the most elevator complaints.
bench.why: It puts elevator breakdowns, which official lookups bury, next to the people responsible for fixing them.
bench.caveat: Tenant-advocacy framing, and its outage estimates assume two hours per complaint.

bench.name: CoreData.nyc
bench.summary: A map and table of every subsidized residential property in the city, from public housing and tax-credit buildings to 421-a, plus more than 100 neighborhood indicators, with a spreadsheet export.
bench.why: The only place to see whether a building is subsidized, under which program and when its affordability rules could expire.
bench.caveat: Built for researchers, so its menus take some learning. The Furman site's "last update" note reads May 2025, though the data behind the map carries 2025 values.

bench.name: Facts About Homelessness
bench.summary: The monthly shelter census in plain figures, with charts of the current month by population and a monthly series back to January 1983.
bench.why: The longest chart of the shelter population anywhere, updated monthly from the city's own reports, with July 2026 figures matching the city's latest.
bench.caveat: An advocacy group with a right-to-shelter stance, and the page frames the numbers that way. No data download.

bench.name: City Owned and Leased Land Maps
bench.summary: Four maps of the city's roughly 15,000 owned or leased parcels: unused, undeveloped, residential (mostly public housing) and other, with details for each lot.
bench.why: An independent look at what the city owns and what is really vacant, alongside the mayor's own LIFT Tracker.
bench.caveat: No data date shown in the tool, and a lot can appear on more than one map.

bench.name: What rezoning built
bench.summary: Every adopted zoning map change since 1977, more than 1,200, joined to the housing completed inside it since 2010, on the city's own upzoned-or-downzoned classification.
bench.why: The only accounting of what rezonings produced: upzoned land yielded about 20 times the homes per acre of downzoned land.
bench.caveat: Classification of rezonings after 2016 is inferred from inclusionary housing areas, which the page discloses.

official.name: Worst Landlord Watchlist
official.summary: An annual ranking of the 100 private landlords with the most open housing code violations, with their buildings mapped.
official.why: A quick, transparent check on the worst actors, with the scoring rules spelled out.
official.caveat: Once a year, top 100 only.

official.maker: Department of Housing Preservation and Development
official.name: HPD Online
official.summary: The city's record for any residential building: complaints, violations, court cases and registration.
official.why: The official source every other building tool draws on.

official.name: ZoLa
official.summary: Click any lot to see its zoning, landmarks, flood zones and pending rezonings.
official.why: The only complete zoning map; no independent tool beats it.

official.name: Sidewalk Shed Map
official.summary: Every permitted sidewalk shed in the city, filterable by how long it has stood, with counts by district.
official.why: Current and simple. On Sept. 28, 2026, it showed 7,134 sheds, up an average of 564 days.

official.name: Housing Production Snapshot
official.summary: An annual map of homes completed and permitted, by borough and neighborhood.
official.why: The clearest official count of all new housing, market-rate and affordable.

official.name: NYCHA Service Interruptions
official.summary: A live list of heat, hot water, elevator, gas and electric outages at public housing developments, with buildings and residents affected and the status of each.
official.why: The only current source on daily conditions in public housing; no independent tool tracks them.
official.caveat: The authority reports on itself, with no download and a page that is hard to read on a phone.

official.maker: Mayor's Office and Housing Preservation and Development
official.name: LIFT Tracker
official.summary: A map of every city-owned or leased property by use, and a pipeline of more than 100 city-owned sites slated for about 50,000 homes, with each project's stage and a method appendix.
official.why: The first public accounting of where the city plans to build on land it already owns.
official.caveat: A mayoral publication with promotional framing, no change log and self-reported project stages.

areas.name: Subways and buses
areas.dek: The MTA publishes monthly performance numbers and live train positions. Independent developers turn those feeds into answers to riders' questions: whether a train is running, how slow a bus is and whether the elevator works.

picks.name: Subway Now
picks.summary: One screen that grades every subway line from the trains' actual movements, with live maps, real waits against scheduled ones and arrival estimates.
picks.why: It catches slowdowns the MTA has not announced, because it measures the trains themselves instead of relaying posted alerts. Free, fast and open source.
questions: Is my train running normally right now?
How long will I actually wait?
picks.caveat: Live only, with no history. Its grades use the developer's own thresholds, not official MTA measures.
picks.data: MTA real-time train positions and schedules
index: Is my train running right now?

picks.name: Bus Speeds by Route
picks.summary: Every MTA bus route ranked by average speed, slowest first, and broken into segments so you can see where each one crawls. The M57 was slowest in June 2026, at 5.1 miles an hour.
picks.why: It turns a large MTA dataset into a list any rider can scan, down to the block where the bus stalls. The coalition report cards that once did this job are gone.
questions: How slow is my bus?
Where on my route does it crawl?
picks.caveat: Included by the editor's judgment: its data runs through June 2026 while the MTA's runs through August. Speeds only, with nothing on bunching or on-time performance.
picks.data: MTA bus route segment speeds
index: How slow is my bus?

picks.name: Transit Access
picks.summary: A live map of every subway station colored by whether its elevators are working, with street elevator locations and planned outages.
picks.why: Far easier to read than the MTA's list of outages, and built by a wheelchair user for riders who depend on elevators.
questions: Is the elevator at my station working?
Is an outage planned at my stop?
picks.caveat: Live status only, so it does not show which elevators fail most. It is only as accurate as the MTA's feed.
picks.data: MTA elevator and escalator outage feeds
index: Is the elevator at my station working?

bench.name: Transit Costs Project
bench.summary: A database of rail projects in more than 50 countries with cost per kilometer, and a case study of New York.
bench.why: The most thorough independent explanation of why building transit here costs so much more than elsewhere.
bench.caveat: Reports and a spreadsheet, not an interactive tool.

bench.name: Subway Data NYC
bench.summary: A daily archive of when every subway train actually arrived at every station since April 2021.
bench.why: The MTA does not publish this history. Journalists and researchers rely on it.
bench.caveat: A dataset for people who work with data.

bench.name: subway.fyi
bench.summary: Live maps that rank stations by wait time and train bunching, a delay radar that flags unusual gaps, and replays of past incidents, from a continuous archive of the MTA's real-time feeds.
bench.why: The deepest live read on how the subway is running at each station.
bench.caveat: Ad-supported and not open source; its delay radar is a prediction, and the site says an official alert follows only about a third of the time.

bench.name: NYC Bus Lane Tracker
bench.summary: Miles of bus lanes by year and borough, measured against the Streets Plan's legal targets, with a map.
bench.why: The clearest scorecard on whether the city is building the bus lanes the law requires.
bench.caveat: Depends on a Transportation Department file that updates irregularly; last refreshed May 2026.

bench.name: Lifts
bench.summary: Every subway elevator and whether it is working right now, with each one's reliability over time, from six MTA feeds.
bench.why: It adds the history Transit Access lacks: which elevators fail most, not only which are out today.
bench.caveat: Live status depends on the MTA's own feeds.

bench.name: All Through the Town
bench.summary: A live map of every bus in service, with route speeds computed from vehicle positions and rolled up by week and month since the tracker began.
bench.why: An independent measure of bus speed that keeps its own history, so changes can be checked against the MTA's figures.
bench.caveat: Speeds are estimates from positions, and read about 9% faster than the MTA's on local routes because stopped buses are dropped.

official.name: MTA Performance Metrics
official.summary: The MTA's dashboards for ridership, subway and bus performance, paratransit, bridges and tunnels and the congestion pricing program.
official.why: The authoritative long-run record, and the most current congestion pricing numbers. Independent congestion pricing trackers have mostly stopped updating.

official.name: Subway Recovery Tracker
official.summary: Monthly ridership at 424 subway stations against a 2017-19 baseline, on a map and in a downloadable spreadsheet through August 2026.
official.why: The only station-by-station view of how ridership has come back since the pandemic.
official.caveat: The written analysis runs months behind the data.

areas.name: Traffic safety, cycling and driving
areas.dek: Crash records, bike lane data and camera tickets are all public. These tools use them to show whether streets are getting safer, whether the city is building what the law requires and which drivers keep breaking the rules. The city's open crash data has not updated since June 11, 2026, so independent crash maps are missing the summer.

picks.name: NYC Crash Mapper
picks.summary: Every police-reported crash since 2011, filterable by district, precinct, intersection or a shape you draw, and by who was hurt. Trend, compare and rank views show how an area has changed.
picks.why: The compare view is the easiest way for anyone to test whether a street redesign cut crashes, and the presentation is plain data.
questions: How many people have been hurt in crashes in my neighborhood?
Did the redesign on my street work?
picks.caveat: Its default view now shows no recent crashes because the city's crash feed stopped after June 11, 2026; pick earlier dates. Built by a pedestrian safety group.
picks.data: Police Department crash records (NYC Open Data)
picks.freshness: Daily when the city feed runs; stuck at June 11, 2026
index: Are the streets in my neighborhood getting safer?

picks.name: How's My Driving NY
picks.summary: Type a license plate to see every parking and camera ticket the city has on file for that vehicle, with fines paid and owed and school-zone speeding streaks.
picks.why: The city's own lookup is built for paying a ticket. This one shows a vehicle's whole record, which is what you want to know about a repeat offender.
questions: How many speed camera tickets does that car have?
Is the car that keeps blocking the bike lane a repeat offender?
picks.caveat: Only as complete as the city's ticket data, which updates on different schedules.
picks.data: Finance Department parking and camera violations
index: How many tickets does that car have?

picks.name: NYC Bike Lane Tracker
picks.summary: Every bike lane segment in the city's data, tallied by year and type and measured against the Streets Plan's legal target of 250 miles of protected lanes from 2022 through 2026. It counted 148 miles as of June 2026.
picks.why: The clearest public scorecard on the city's biggest legally required street safety commitment, built from the city's own data, with each new segment dated and mapped.
questions: Is the city building the bike lanes the law requires?
What bike lanes went in near me this year?
picks.caveat: It counts lanes the city has logged as installed, so it can lag construction, and a two-way lane counts twice. The maker writes from a street safety point of view.
picks.data: Transportation Department bike route data
index: Is the city meeting its bike lane target?

bench.name: CrashCount
bench.summary: Crash, injury and death counts for more than 500 districts and neighborhoods, a lookup for any address, and fatal crashes confirmed by the press before police records arrive.
bench.why: The friendliest crash lookup, and its press-confirmed deaths partly fill the gap left by the frozen city feed.
bench.caveat: Included by the editor's judgment: its makers describe themselves only as "a small team of New Yorkers." Openly advocacy in tone, and its death counts mix press reports with police data.

bench.name: ctbk.dev
bench.summary: Citi Bike rides per month since 2014, station maps with common destinations and a record of when each station sat empty or full.
bench.why: The empty-and-full history answers a common rider complaint that Citi Bike does not publish.

bench.name: How is NYC Parking Enforcement?
bench.summary: Search any block, precinct or agency to see the parking tickets written there, including on the blocks around each station house.
bench.why: It shows whether anyone enforces parking rules on a given block, which no city tool does.
bench.caveat: Street names are spelled inconsistently in the source data, so a street can appear under several names.

official.name: Vision Zero View
official.summary: The city's map of traffic injuries and deaths, with street design changes and speed limits layered on.
official.why: With the public crash feed frozen, it is the only source with crash totals through August 2026.

areas.name: 311, trash, rats and parks
areas.dek: 311 takes millions of requests a year, and the city publishes every one. These tools show how satisfied callers are with the city's response, where the public spaces are and whether composting is catching on. For rats, trees and snow, the government's own maps are the best available.

picks.name: NYC 311 Report Card
picks.summary: Letter grades for every city agency and complaint type, built from the surveys the city sends people after it closes a 311 request. Pick a month, three months or a year, then drill into an agency.
picks.why: It measures what 311 callers think of the city's response, from the city's own survey data, which no official page grades this way. Streetsblog has cited it.
questions: Which agencies handle 311 complaints worst?
Is the city getting better at answering 311?
picks.caveat: People who answer the survey choose to, and response rates are low. It measures satisfaction, not response time.
picks.data: 311 service requests and the 311 resolution satisfaction survey (NYC Open Data)
index: How well does the city answer 311 complaints?

picks.name: NYC Public Space
picks.summary: One map of about 2,800 public spaces that the city otherwise lists agency by agency: parks, street plazas, privately owned public spaces, waterfront walkways and schoolyards opened as playgrounds. Tap a space for its type, managing agency and details.
picks.why: It is the only place that shows every kind of public space together, including the privately owned plazas and waterfront areas the public has a legal right to use. Gothamist has covered it.
questions: Where is a public plaza or park I can sit in near here?
Is that plaza or waterfront walkway actually public?
picks.caveat: Some additions come from AI-assisted research and user submissions rather than agency records, and its downloadable data snapshot is a year old.
picks.data: Parks, Transportation and City Planning public-space data (NYC Open Data)
index: Where can I find public space near me?

picks.maker: Brooklyn and Manhattan Solid Waste Advisory Boards
picks.name: Track NYC Trash
picks.summary: Monthly estimates of how much compost and recycling each community district captures, and a second dashboard on where the city's garbage goes after pickup, by route, site and cost.
picks.why: It shows whether curbside composting is working, district by district, in a way the Sanitation Department does not, with definitions and sources spelled out.
questions: Is composting catching on in my district?
Where does the city's garbage go?
picks.caveat: Capture rates are estimates that lean on a 2023 waste study. The boards say they use the data for advocacy as well as education.
picks.data: Sanitation Department monthly tonnage and waste export data
index: Is composting working in my neighborhood?

bench.maker: Maker not named on the site
bench.name: 311 Wrapped
bench.summary: Enter a ZIP code for a year in review of 311 reports: top complaints, busiest hours, how fast complaints close and how this year compares with last.
bench.why: A careful, published method in a format people will click through.
bench.caveat: Included by the editor's judgment: the site does not name its maker. Its scores and grades are its own judgments.

bench.name: ParkScore: New York
bench.summary: Scores the city's park system on acreage, access, spending, amenities and equity, and compares park space by neighborhood income and race.
bench.why: A current national yardstick with a clear equity lens.
bench.caveat: City-level scores with little neighborhood detail.

bench.name: 311 Parking Complaints That End in a Summons
bench.summary: The share of 311 illegal-parking complaints the Police Department closes as "summons issued," by month, borough and type, from blocked bike lanes to sidewalk parking.
bench.why: It shows how often a parking complaint leads to a ticket, according to the police's own closing codes.
bench.caveat: The closing codes cannot be checked against actual tickets.

bench.name: Sound and the city
bench.summary: Every 311 noise complaint this year and last on a map, with the noise-code tickets the city actually wrote and a "last Saturday night" view, refreshed daily.
bench.why: It sets complaints beside enforcement, which no city page does.
bench.caveat: Complaints measure who calls 311, not noise.

official.name: NYC311 Monitoring Tool
official.summary: 311 complaints by neighborhood, ZIP code and borough: the top complaint types last month, the change from the month before and trends back to 2019.
official.why: The clearest current count of what each neighborhood complains about, from an office independent of the agencies being complained about.
questions: What do people in my neighborhood complain about most?
Are noise complaints going up where I live?
official.caveat: It counts complaints, not conditions, so it partly measures who calls 311. It does not show how fast the city responds.
index: What does my neighborhood complain about?

official.name: Rat Information Portal
official.summary: Every Health Department rat inspection, mapped building by building, with each property's history.
official.why: The authoritative record, current to within days. We found no credible independent rat tool.

official.name: NYC Tree Map
official.summary: Nearly 893,000 trees managed by the Parks Department, each with species, size and care history.
official.why: The definitive street tree map, current and tied to volunteer care.

official.name: PlowNYC
official.summary: During snowstorms, when a plow or salt spreader last passed each street.
official.why: Street-by-street accountability for snow response. Idle outside storms.

areas.name: Flooding, heat and the water
areas.dek: Climate risk in New York City is block by block: one street floods and the next stays dry. These tools run on their own sensors and water samples, which is why they can show conditions street by street. The Health Department's portal covers air quality and heat vulnerability.

picks.maker: New York University and CUNY, with city agencies
picks.name: FloodNet
picks.summary: A map of street flood sensors across the five boroughs showing current water depth and each sensor's record of past floods.
picks.why: The only live, block-level measure of street flooding in the city, and it shows which intersections flood again and again.
questions: Is my street flooding right now?
How deep did the water get in the last storm?
picks.caveat: It only sees where sensors are installed, so a quiet map does not mean a dry city.
picks.data: FloodNet street sensors, also shared on NYC Open Data
index: Is my street flooding?

picks.name: NYC Urban Heat Portal
picks.summary: A neighborhood map of outdoor heat exposure built from surface temperature, tree canopy, cool roofs and pavement, with a profile scoring each factor and counts of extreme heat days.
picks.why: It shows why a neighborhood runs hot, factor by factor, in plain profiles with downloadable data.
questions: How hot does my neighborhood get?
Why is my block hotter than others?
picks.caveat: Included by the editor's judgment: its data covers 2013 to 2023 and it was last updated in May 2025. For who is most at risk in a heat wave, use the Health Department's heat vulnerability index.
picks.data: Satellite temperature imagery, weather stations, tree canopy and roof data
index: Why is my neighborhood so hot?

picks.name: NYC Water Check
picks.summary: The latest sewage-bacteria reading at about 80 shoreline sites, how each compares with its usual level, and trends by borough.
picks.why: It answers whether the water is safe for swimming or kayaking this week, which no official page does for the whole shoreline, and it explains its method.
questions: Is the water at my pier safe to kayak in this week?
Does it get dirtier after rain?
picks.caveat: Built by one person on volunteer sampling rather than government data. By its own published tests, its rain-based model calls the swim threshold right 64.8% of the time, against 77.3% for a simple 48-hour rain rule; the sample readings themselves are measurements.
picks.data: Community water quality sampling; rainfall records
index: Is the harbor clean enough to swim in?

bench.name: Water Quality Portal
bench.summary: Pass-fail bacteria results at sampling sites since 2008, with nearby sources of pollution.
bench.why: A long record from an established watchdog group.
bench.caveat: Focused on the Hudson, and the latest sample dates were not shown.

official.name: Environment & Health Data Portal
official.summary: Neighborhood reports and data on air quality, heat vulnerability, asthma, lead, housing conditions and health.
official.why: The best official data site in the city: well explained, current and neighborhood-level.

areas.name: Schools and children
areas.dek: The Education Department publishes report cards and admissions data for every school, in forms built for administrators. These tools repackage the same numbers for families, and one adds admissions records obtained through public records requests.

picks.maker: Center for New York City Affairs, The New School
picks.name: InsideSchools
picks.summary: Profiles of public schools from pre-K through high school that pair city and state data, such as test scores, chronic absence and survey results, with reviews written after school visits, plus plain guides to admissions.
picks.why: It answers the question families have, whether a school is right for their child, by adding context to the same data the official report cards use.
questions: Is my zoned school any good?
How many kids at this school are chronically absent?
picks.caveat: Written reviews are not refreshed on a schedule; one we checked dated to 2019. Partly supported by advertising.
picks.data: Education Department school quality, survey and demographic data; state test results
index: Is my zoned school any good?

picks.maker: A New York City parent, not named on the site
picks.name: NYC-SIFT
picks.summary: A free search of more than 400 high schools and 900 programs showing applicants per seat, admissions cutoffs and estimated odds, from more than 20 Education Department datasets and records obtained through public records requests.
picks.why: It publishes admissions numbers the city does not gather in one place and turns them into odds a parent can read.
questions: How hard is it to get into this high school?
How many kids applied for each seat?
picks.caveat: Included by the editor's judgment: the maker is named only as a New York City father. High school only, and school pages carry AI-written summaries.
picks.data: Education Department admissions and school data; records obtained under the Freedom of Information Law
picks.freshness: Current for the fall 2026 admissions cycle
index: What are my kid's odds at a high school?

picks.name: Schools Finder
picks.summary: One profile per public school combining the city's School Quality Report, enrollment snapshot and admissions directories, with each figure's definition, period and source. It gives no overall score.
picks.why: The cleanest single profile of any public school, refreshed automatically and careful about what each number means.
questions: How does my kid's school compare with similar schools?
Who goes to this school?
picks.caveat: New in August 2026, built by one developer, in English only.
picks.data: Education Department school quality, enrollment and admissions data
index: How does this school compare?

picks.maker: Citizens' Committee for Children of New York
picks.name: Keeping Track Online
picks.summary: Hundreds of measures of how children and families are doing, including poverty, food stamps, early intervention and child welfare services, by community district, school district, precinct and ZIP code.
picks.why: The deepest neighborhood data on children in the city, kept current by a research staff. New food stamp figures went up in May 2026.
questions: How many kids in my district live in poverty?
Where are families using child welfare services?
picks.caveat: The interface is dated, and some figures are estimates converted from larger Census areas. The committee is a child advocacy group.
picks.data: Census, Education, Homeless Services and Health Department data; state benefit records
index: How are children doing in my neighborhood?

bench.name: School Utilization Map
bench.summary: Every school's enrollment against its capacity on a map, with tables on whether each school meets the class size law.
bench.why: The only place that maps crowding school by school while the class size law is phased in.
bench.caveat: An advocacy group campaigning for smaller classes. The map shows 2024-25.

bench.name: Educational Opportunity Project
bench.summary: Test results for every school district in the country, including the city's, on a common scale, with learning rates, pandemic recovery and segregation measures.
bench.why: The credible way to compare city districts with the rest of the country, updated September 2026.
bench.caveat: Built for researchers.

bench.maker: Center for New York City Affairs, The New School
bench.name: Watching the Numbers
bench.summary: An annual report on the child protective system: investigations, services and foster care over six years.
bench.why: The clearest independent read on the Administration for Children's Services.
bench.caveat: A report, not a tool.

official.name: School Quality Reports
official.summary: The official report card for every school, with test results, attendance, survey results and comparisons.
official.why: The authoritative source the independent sites build on.

areas.name: Health
areas.dek: No independent tool passed our tests here. The Health Department publishes reports and indicators, and hospitals answer to state and federal regulators, but nobody outside government has built a current tool on overdoses, mental health or hospital performance for the city. What follows is the government's own, plus one national hospital grader. The Health Department's Environment & Health Data Portal, under Climate, covers asthma, lead, life expectancy and heat.

bench.name: Leapfrog Hospital Safety Grade
bench.summary: Letter grades for general hospitals nationwide, including the city's, from up to 32 patient-safety measures such as infections, falls and medication errors, reissued every spring and fall.
bench.why: The only current, plain-language grade for the safety of a specific hospital.
bench.caveat: A national tool, not built on city data, and hospitals can decline the survey behind it.

official.name: Respiratory Illness Data
official.summary: Weekly charts of emergency room visits, hospitalizations, cases and deaths for COVID-19, flu and RSV, with the files posted on GitHub.
official.why: The current answer to whether COVID, flu or RSV is going around, updated every Thursday.
official.caveat: Preliminary counts that can change; emergency room data miss people who do not go to one.

official.name: Maternal and Child Health Dashboard
official.summary: Seventy-six maternal, infant and child health measures, including maternal mortality, for the state and each county, so each borough, with trend charts and downloads.
official.why: The only current source on maternal and infant health by borough, with its methods explained.
official.caveat: Counties, not neighborhoods, and some measures lag to 2022.

official.maker: Mayor's Office of Community Mental Health
official.name: B-HEARD data
official.summary: Charts and tables on the program that sends mental health teams instead of police to some 911 calls: calls eligible and routed, outcomes and satisfaction, by fiscal year.
official.why: The only public numbers on the city's mental health crisis response.
official.caveat: Self-reported by the program's own office, covers only the precincts it operates in, and runs a year behind.

areas.name: Budget and spending
areas.dek: The city spends well over $100 billion a year, and its spending, contracts and payroll are public, mostly through the comptroller's Checkbook NYC, listed below under "From the government." The independent tools here explain the budget, show what pensions cost and what city jobs pay. We found no current independent tool on tax breaks or city debt.

picks.name: NYC Budget Explorer
picks.summary: Every agency's budget from fiscal 2017 through 2027, comparing what was adopted with what was later changed, with drill-downs and a downloadable file.
picks.why: The clearest independent view of where the money goes and how that has shifted, with a documented method that matches the city's totals.
questions: How much does the city spend on police, schools or sanitation?
Has an agency's budget grown since 2017?
picks.caveat: New in July 2026 and coded with AI help, so how well it will be kept up is unknown. It shows budgeted dollars, not actual spending.
picks.data: City expense budget (NYC Open Data)
index: How much does each agency get?

picks.name: NYC Property Tax Map
picks.summary: Every property in the city colored by its effective tax rate. Search an address to see its tax bill and compare it with the neighbors'.
picks.why: It answers whether your property tax is fair far better than the Finance Department's own portal, which shows one lot at a time with no comparison.
questions: Is my property tax rate higher than my neighbors'?
Why do some expensive homes pay lower rates?
picks.caveat: Included by the editor's judgment: it still shows the 2025-26 tax year, and the 2026-27 roll is out. The maker argues for reform, though the numbers come straight from city data.
picks.data: Finance Department assessment and tax data
index: Is my property tax fair?

picks.name: What New York owes
picks.summary: A ledger of New York City's five public pension funds: what they hold, what they owe, what the city pays in each year and what the gap works out to per household, fiscal 2013 to 2025. Tabs let you compare the five funds, follow the funded ratio over time, run scenarios and read the method.
picks.why: It is the only current independent look at what the city's five pension funds cost taxpayers; other sources cover only how the investments did.
questions: How much does New York City owe its retired workers, and how much has it set aside?
How much of the city budget goes to pensions each year?
picks.caveat: Annual accounting snapshots measured at market value on one day a year; the scenario tab is a simplification, not an actuarial valuation.
picks.data: NYC Office of the Actuary pension reports and the Comptroller's annual financial report, fiscal 2013 to 2025
picks.freshness: Annual, with the fiscal 2025 financial reports
index: What do city pensions cost?

picks.name: The Pay Gap
picks.summary: The city payroll by job title or agency since fiscal 2014: median pay, overtime and tenure, adjusted for New York prices and rent. It deliberately has no search by name.
picks.why: It answers what city jobs pay, and whether pay has kept up with local costs, without turning into a list of individual workers' salaries.
questions: What does a city bus operator or nurse earn?
Has city pay kept up with rent?
picks.caveat: Gender figures are estimated from first names. One developer, and the maker is named only in the code repository.
picks.data: Citywide payroll data (NYC Open Data); federal price data
picks.freshness: Annual; fiscal 2025, the newest year the city has published
index: What do city workers earn?

bench.name: NYC Council Discretionary Funding
bench.summary: Where the City Council's discretionary money goes, fiscal 2015 through 2027, by category and initiative. The fiscal 2027 total is about $656 million.
bench.why: The only independent, reconciled view of the money Council members steer to local groups.

bench.name: SeeThroughNY
bench.summary: Names, titles and pay of city employees, plus a database of retirees' pensions.
bench.why: The quickest way to answer what a city job pays or who earned the most overtime.
bench.caveat: Data runs through fiscal 2025. The Empire Center is a free-market think tank.

bench.name: Databook.NYC
bench.summary: Cross-linked profiles of city agencies, employees, job titles, capital projects, contracts and vendors, plus a daily digest of City Record notices.
bench.why: The best general-purpose explorer of city government data, updated daily.
bench.caveat: Dense; best for people who know what they are looking for.

bench.name: NYC municipal labor contracts
bench.summary: The full text of every collective bargaining agreement in force for city employees, scanned and searchable, with pages on bargaining units and the wage pattern.
bench.why: The contracts that set pay and rules for more than 300,000 city workers, searchable for the first time in one place.
bench.caveat: Many source PDFs are scans, so the text can carry recognition errors; check quotes against the linked originals.

bench.name: The fully loaded budget
bench.summary: The fiscal 2027 adopted budget with pensions, benefits, debt service and legal settlements assigned to the agencies they belong to, so each agency's real cost shows.
bench.why: The city budgets those costs in central pools; this is the only view that puts them where the spending happens, and it reconciles to the printed total.
bench.caveat: Budgeted figures for a year not yet audited; actual spending will differ.

official.name: Checkbook NYC
official.summary: A searchable ledger of the city's day-to-day finances: budget, revenue, every check, registered contracts and payroll, by agency, vendor and year.
official.why: Nothing independent comes close on the basic question of where the money goes, and it is close to real time. It showed $38.7 billion spent so far in fiscal 2027 on Sept. 28, 2026.
questions: Which companies and nonprofits does the city pay, and how much?
Who holds the biggest contracts at an agency?
official.caveat: Built for depth, not ease, and full of budget jargon. Its bot protection turns away some privacy browsers and VPNs.
official.data: Comptroller's Office budget, spending, contract and payroll records
index: Who does the city pay, and how much?

official.name: NYC Budget Resources
official.summary: The Independent Budget Office's plain-language hub: Budget 101, a glossary, charts of spending and staffing by agency since 1980, a monthly snapshot of the budget and workforce, and a graphic that shrinks the budget to $100.
official.why: The best starting point for someone who wants the budget explained rather than a database to search, from the city's nonpartisan budget analysts.
questions: How big is the city budget and what does it pay for?
How has spending at an agency changed since 1980?
official.caveat: The charts load slowly and are hard to link to one at a time.
official.data: City financial plans, adopted budgets and the city's financial management system
official.freshness: Monthly snapshot; data as of Sept. 8, 2026
index: How does the city budget work?

official.name: NYC Agency Staffing Dashboard
official.summary: Authorized positions against actual employees for every agency each month since 2012, with vacancy rates. It counted 292,808 employees and 14,391 vacancies as of Aug. 31, 2026.
official.why: The best answer to which agencies are short-staffed, updated monthly.

official.name: Late Contracts Dashboard
official.summary: How late the city registers its contracts, by agency, vendor and industry, since 2011.
official.why: The only tool on the delays that leave nonprofits working for months before they are paid.
official.caveat: Measures registration, not payment, and the comptroller's office is part of the registration process.

official.name: Property Information Portal
official.summary: The official lookup for any lot's assessed value, exemptions, abatements and tax map.
official.why: Where every property tax question ends; pair it with the tax map above.

official.name: Discretionary Award Tracker
official.summary: The status of every City Council discretionary award from the past three fiscal years.
official.why: Shows whether Council money promised to a local group has made it through the contract process.

areas.name: Council, community boards and elections
areas.dek: Most decisions that shape a block pass through a community board, the City Council or the ballot box. The official records are scattered across Legistar, 59 board websites and YouTube. These tools gather them up and make them searchable.

picks.name: Block Party
picks.summary: A searchable archive of about 12,000 community board meeting transcripts and nearly 40,000 board resolutions, each with a short summary of what was asked and how the board voted.
picks.why: Nothing else lets you search what community boards decide across boards. Summaries sit next to the full text so you can check them, and new meetings appear within days.
questions: What did my community board decide about that liquor license?
Has my board ever voted on bike lanes on my street?
picks.caveat: Coverage is uneven: resolutions come from 27 boards in Brooklyn and Manhattan, transcripts from about 40 boards that post video. Summaries are written by AI.
picks.data: Community board meeting videos and posted resolutions
index: What did my community board decide?

picks.name: intro.nyc
picks.summary: Fast search of City Council bills since 2014, with sponsors, status, short shareable links and a feed of the past month's actions. Other pages list members, local laws by year and hearings.
picks.why: It is far quicker and easier to read than Legistar, the Council's official system, and its data updates daily and is open to anyone.
questions: Is there a Council bill about e-bikes?
What has my Council member sponsored?
picks.caveat: A one-person volunteer project. It covers bills, not what happens after a law passes.
picks.data: City Council legislative records (Legistar)
index: Is the Council working on a bill about something I care about?

picks.maker: CUNY Center for Urban Research and League of Women Voters
picks.name: Who Represents Me? NYC
picks.summary: Type an address and get every elected official who represents it, from Council member to members of Congress, plus the community board, with office phone numbers.
picks.why: One lookup covers every level of government, from a university mapping center and a nonpartisan civic group. It uses exact addresses rather than ZIP codes, which can straddle districts.
questions: Who is my Council member?
Which community board am I in?
picks.caveat: No as-of date is shown for the rosters, though they were current when we checked.
picks.data: League of Women Voters officeholder lists; city and state district boundaries
picks.freshness: Current as of a Sept. 28, 2026 check
index: Who represents me?

bench.name: NYC Election Atlas
bench.summary: City election results mapped by election district, including the ranked-choice rounds of the 2025 mayoral primary and the 2025 general election against 2021.
bench.why: The clearest way to see how neighborhoods voted, from a university mapping center with a long record.
bench.caveat: Updated after major elections; no 2026 maps yet.

bench.name: NYC Civic Calendar
bench.summary: Pick community boards, Council committees and agency hearing bodies, and their meetings drop into your phone's calendar.
bench.why: It handles the hardest part of showing up, knowing when and where, for 347 public bodies.
bench.caveat: Depends on reading board websites, so gaps appear when a board changes its site.

bench.name: CB Member Tracker
bench.summary: Who chairs and manages each of the 59 community boards, with published member rosters and the term limits that will force turnover in 2027.
bench.why: The only citywide roster of community board leadership, candid about which boards publish what.

bench.maker: Anna Bao, James Carroll, Dev Doshi and Michael Sheehan
bench.name: CityScroll
bench.summary: City Record notices, contracts, land-use applications, rules, meetings and civil service exams in one feed, searchable by neighborhood, Council district, agency or topic, each linked to its official source.
bench.why: The easiest way to see what the city is doing near you across dozens of official notice streams, with alerts by email or calendar.
bench.caveat: New in summer 2026 and built by volunteers; its plain-language summaries are AI-written with human review.

bench.name: 9/11 City Records
bench.summary: The 9/11 documents the city Law Department began releasing in 2026, searchable by building, timeline, topic and agency, with page-level links back to the official files.
bench.why: It makes a huge new document release usable one building at a time.
bench.caveat: Covers one document release, relies on scanned text, and its machine-written answers can be wrong, as the site says.

bench.name: citymeetings.nyc
bench.summary: City Council hearings from August 2023 to May 2025 broken into short, titled chapters with summaries, so you can jump to a single exchange in a 10-hour hearing. Also covers the 2025 Charter Revision Commission.
bench.why: The best-edited archive of Council hearings for 2024 and early 2025, with human review of the AI transcripts.
bench.caveat: Included by the editor's judgment: it has covered almost no hearings since May 2025, so it is an archive, not a current source.

bench.name: The Greener Book
bench.summary: The city's official directory of officials, agencies, addresses and press offices, about 3,000 records, rebuilt as one search box and kept current from the City Record.
bench.why: Faster than the city's own Green Book Online, with every phone number a tap away and a flag when the directory disagrees with the City Record.
bench.caveat: The listings are the city's; the disagreement flags are computed, not official findings.

official.name: Follow the Money
official.summary: Every contribution, expenditure and public matching payment for city candidates, plus spending by outside groups, searchable and mapped.
official.why: The authoritative source on money in city races; no independent tool improves on it.
official.caveat: Spread across several older interfaces.

official.name: NYC Lobbyist Search
official.summary: Lobbyist registrations and reports, searchable by lobbyist, client, subject and the officials targeted.
official.why: The only place to see who is lobbying City Hall; we found no independent alternative.

official.name: Find My Poll Site
official.summary: Enter an address for your early voting and Election Day poll sites and a sample ballot.
official.why: The authoritative answer to where you vote and what is on the ballot.

official.name: Election Results
official.summary: Certified results for every contest, including the June 2026 primary, as summaries and election-district files in PDF and spreadsheet form, plus the full cast vote record and an archive back to 2004.
official.why: The source for the June 2026 primary, which no independent map has drawn yet.
official.caveat: Tables and files, no maps.

official.name: 2025 Voter Analysis Report
official.summary: The board's annual report on the 2025 elections: turnout by community district, registration and matching-funds figures, with highlights on the web page and the full report as a PDF.
official.why: The best account of who voted in the 2025 mayoral election and where.
official.caveat: A report rather than a tool; sources and method sit in the PDF's footnotes.

areas.name: Neighborhoods and people
areas.dek: Census and city data can describe any neighborhood in detail, and the city's archives hold photos of nearly every building. These tools make both usable without a data background, from a district profile with 25 years of history to the tax photo of your own building.

picks.name: NYC Neighborhood Data Profiles
picks.summary: One page per community district with tables and charts on population, income, rents, rent burden, code violations, home sales, permits, subsidized housing and serious crime, most back to 2000. Each chart's data downloads as a spreadsheet.
picks.why: The most authoritative single profile of a neighborhood in the city, from a university research center, with 2024 census figures and 2025 city records.
questions: How much has rent gone up in my neighborhood since 2010?
How many apartments were built near me, and how many were income-restricted?
picks.caveat: Census estimates at the community district scale carry real sampling error, and the page does not print margins of error.
picks.data: Census, Buildings, Housing Preservation and Development, Finance and Police Department records
index: How has my neighborhood changed since 2000?

picks.maker: Measure of America, Social Science Research Council
picks.name: DATA2GO.NYC
picks.summary: More than 400 measures of well-being, from life expectancy to college degrees, mapped and ranked for boroughs, community districts, neighborhoods and census tracts.
picks.why: It answers how a neighborhood is doing across health, income, schools and housing in one place, which no single city tool does.
questions: How does life expectancy in my neighborhood compare?
Where are poverty and poor health concentrated?
picks.caveat: Included by the editor's judgment: its census figures are one release behind (2019-23, with 2020-24 out). Most measures run two to four years behind, and it works best on a large screen.
picks.data: Census, Health Department vital statistics, state education data and more
index: How is my neighborhood doing?

picks.name: Census Reporter
picks.summary: Readable profiles of the city, its boroughs, neighborhoods, ZIP codes and census tracts, with each figure compared in plain English to the region, state and nation.
picks.why: It answers who lives here faster and more clearly than the city's Population FactFinder, and it works on a phone.
questions: Who lives in my neighborhood?
Is my ZIP code richer or poorer than the city?
picks.caveat: Uses census geographies rather than neighborhood names, and small areas carry wide margins of error.
picks.data: Census Bureau American Community Survey and 2020 Census
index: Who lives in my neighborhood?

picks.name: 1940s.nyc
picks.summary: The Municipal Archives' 1939-41 tax photos of nearly every building in the five boroughs, placed on a street map. Zoom to any block and click a dot to see the photo.
picks.why: A model of turning a city record into something anyone can use, and it answers a question people ask about their own block.
questions: What did my building look like around 1940?
What stood on my block before?
picks.caveat: Photos were placed automatically, and some may be in the wrong spot.
picks.data: Municipal Archives tax photographs, 1939-41
index: What did my block look like in 1940?

bench.name: 80s.NYC
bench.summary: The Finance Department's mid-1980s photos of every property, viewable street by street.
bench.why: The companion to 1940s.nyc, and a vivid record of the city before its recent building booms.
bench.caveat: Low-resolution images captured from video discs.

bench.name: Mapping Historical New York
bench.summary: Six and a half million census records from 1850, 1880 and 1910, each person placed at a home address in Manhattan and Brooklyn, with layers for birthplace, occupation and density.
bench.why: The only block-by-block picture of who lived where in the 19th-century city, with its method published.
bench.caveat: Manhattan and Brooklyn only, three census years, and federal rather than city records.

official.name: Population FactFinder
official.summary: Census profiles for any neighborhood, community district or area you draw, with change over time.
official.why: The official source on city demographics, with geographies built for New York City.
official.caveat: Desktop only.

areas.name: Immigrants and newcomers
areas.dek: About four in ten New Yorkers were born abroad, and the city's immigration courts carry one of the largest backlogs in the country. The tools here are built on federal court and enforcement records, obtained through public records requests, and on the city's own count of who speaks what. Migrants in the shelter system are covered under Housing.

picks.name: Immigration Court Backlog
picks.summary: Pending immigration court cases by court, nationality, charge and year, from 1998 through August 2026. Pick New York, then a court, to see the city's caseload and how long cases wait; companion tools cover new filings, outcomes, asylum and bond decisions.
picks.why: The only current, independent count of the city's immigration court backlog, from records the university obtained under the Freedom of Information Act.
questions: How many deportation cases are pending in the city's immigration courts?
How long do people wait for a hearing at 26 Federal Plaza?
picks.caveat: A national site; you reach New York City by picking the state and a court. Bulk data cost money, though the query tools are free.
picks.data: Immigration court records from the Justice Department, obtained under the Freedom of Information Act
index: How big is the immigration court backlog here?

bench.maker: UC Berkeley and UCLA law schools
bench.name: Deportation Data Project
bench.summary: Individual-level records of immigration arrests, detentions and removals obtained through public records lawsuits, charted by month and filterable by state and enforcement area, with the full datasets downloadable.
bench.why: The most detailed public record of federal immigration enforcement, with a codebook and the raw files.
bench.caveat: National, and the newest release lacks the field that once identified the New York enforcement area. Data run several months behind.

official.name: NYC Language Explorer
official.summary: Maps and charts of New Yorkers with limited English by language, for the city, each borough and each community district, with margins of error shown.
official.why: The clearest official answer to which languages your neighbors speak, built for the city's language-access law.
official.caveat: The tool does not say which census years it uses.

areas.name: Jobs, the economy and poverty
areas.dek: Independent tools are scarce here. These cover city jobs, the cost of living and poverty. The most current monthly reads on the economy come from the two comptrollers' offices, listed under "From the government."

picks.name: NYC Civil Service Exams
picks.summary: Every city civil service exam that is open, coming or closed, with application dates, the salary range for the title and how often agencies have hired from its list.
picks.why: The easiest way to find a city job exam and see whether its list actually leads to jobs, refreshed daily.
questions: Which city civil service exams are open now?
Is the list for my exam still being used?
picks.caveat: New in August 2026 and built by one developer. The city never published the July 2024 to June 2025 exam schedule as open data, so those exams are missing.
picks.data: Citywide Administrative Services exam schedules; civil service list data (NYC Open Data)
index: How do I get a city job?

picks.name: Poverty Tracker
