picks.summary: An annual report from a survey that follows the same New Yorkers over time, measuring poverty and hardship. The March 2026 edition found 2.2 million New Yorkers in poverty in 2024.
picks.why: It captures hardship and movement in and out of poverty that one-time government snapshots miss, and it is the most-cited independent poverty figure in the city.
questions: How many New Yorkers live in poverty?
How much do benefits keep people out of poverty?
picks.caveat: Built on its own survey, not government data, and delivered as reports. Robin Hood funds and advocates on the issues it measures.
picks.data: Poverty Tracker survey of city residents
index: How many New Yorkers are poor?

picks.name: Living Wage Calculator
picks.summary: The hourly wage needed to cover basic needs for 12 household types in each borough, with typical costs itemized.
picks.why: The freshest easy answer to what it costs to live here, updated February 2026.
picks.caveat: A national tool built mostly on federal data; borough averages hide big differences in rent.
questions: How much do I need to earn to live in Brooklyn?
How far is the minimum wage from a living wage here?
picks.data: Federal cost-of-living data
index: What does it cost to live here?

bench.name: State of the Chains
bench.summary: An annual count of national chain stores in the city by borough and ZIP code. The 2025 edition found a net loss of 112 stores.
bench.why: The most reliable recurring measure of storefront change from an independent source.
bench.caveat: Counts chains only, from the center's own tally.

official.name: New York by the Numbers
official.summary: A monthly briefing on the city's economy and finances, with charts on jobs by industry, unemployment, inflation, the office market, housing construction and tax collections.
official.why: The most current plain-language read on the local economy each month, from an office independent of the mayor. Every issue since 2020 is archived.
questions: Is the city adding or losing jobs?
What is the unemployment rate here?
official.caveat: A newsletter, not an interactive tool, and each issue carries the comptroller's framing.
official.data: Federal and state labor statistics; city tax and housing data
index: Is the city gaining or losing jobs?

official.name: New York City Industry Sector Dashboards
official.summary: Employment, wages and other measures for eight industries, from restaurants and retail to tourism and securities, compared with the state and nation.
official.why: The best interactive look at how specific industries are doing, from an independent state watchdog.
questions: Are restaurant and retail jobs back?
What do jobs in each industry pay?
official.caveat: The text still frames everything around the pandemic recovery, and pages show no update date.
official.data: State Labor Department employment and wage data; state taxable sales
index: How are restaurants and stores doing?

official.maker: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
official.name: Regional Employment Trends
official.summary: Monthly payroll jobs since 2000 for the city and 20 other areas.
official.why: The best single chart of city job counts over 25 years.

official.name: NYC Poverty Atlas
official.summary: Charts, tables and maps of the city's own poverty measure through 2024, which uses a local poverty line and counts benefits.
official.why: A new, plain-language home for the city's most rigorous poverty numbers.

gaps.q: What do the district attorneys do with cases?
gaps.note: Manhattan's data dashboard has been "under construction" since 2024, the Bronx's will not load and the other three boroughs have none.

gaps.q: How long does an ambulance take in my neighborhood?
gaps.note: The city's 911 dashboard gives citywide averages only. No independent tool breaks response times down by neighborhood.

gaps.q: How much overtime are police officers working?
gaps.note: The Police Department posts quarterly spreadsheets; nothing turns them into a lookup or a trend.

gaps.q: Which buildings get tax breaks, and what do they cost?
gaps.note: No current tool tracks 421-a, J-51 and other tax expenditures building by building.

gaps.q: How much does the city owe, and what does its debt cost?
gaps.note: Only the comptroller's financial report tables and the Independent Budget Office's history cover city debt.

gaps.q: Are overdose deaths rising in my neighborhood?
gaps.note: The Health Department publishes reports; no independent tool tracks overdoses or mental health services by neighborhood.
The Council's analysis is from 2022, Vacant New York is gone and the Manhattan Chamber's tracker covers one borough on private data.

gaps.q: Does my public housing building have heat and hot water today?
gaps.note: NYCHA's own outage page, listed under Housing, is the only source. No independent tool tracks daily conditions.

gaps.q: Did congestion pricing thin out traffic, and is it holding?
gaps.note: Every independent tracker stopped updating in 2025. The MTA's own dashboard is the current source.

gaps.q: What was said at last week's Council hearing?
gaps.note: citymeetings.nyc, which summarized hearings chapter by chapter, has covered almost nothing since May 2025.

gaps.q: How did my election district vote in June?
gaps.note: The Board of Elections publishes results by election district, listed under Civics, but no independent map has drawn the 2026 primary yet.

gaps.q: Is my building on track for the city's carbon limits?
gaps.note: The city's address lookup for Local Law 97 is stuck on 2022 data, and two university energy maps have gone offline.

gaps.q: How are the ferries, the commuter railroads and Access-A-Ride doing?
gaps.note: The MTA publishes some of this, but no independent tool covers transit beyond the subway and buses.

gaps.q: How are the libraries and cultural institutions doing?
gaps.note: Nothing we found tracks branch hours, use or cultural funding.

changelog.note: Second cut: every tool re-checked against the two tests. 23 came off, 18 independent tools and Vital City's crime dashboards went on, and government tools moved to their own shelf.
Nine of Josh Greenman's tools, which had failed only for lacking a byline, got one and joined the list.

Added Start here, browsing by agency and a list of questions no tool answers well. Fourteen tools that failed one test went on the list by the editor's judgment, each saying what it is missing. A third research round covered newsrooms, research institutions and uncovered subjects, and added two areas, immigration and health.
